svg.text: Building the swizzled layout of shared memory, line by line
A layout maps a spot (row, column) of a tile to a slot: a position in the buffer, counted in values. Shared memory is cut into
32 banks of 4 bytes; a 16-byte chunk of a row covers 4 banks. Blue: chunk c0, the chunk one load reads from 8 rows at once.
How wide is one row of the pattern?

svg.text: 32 values × 2 bytes = 64 bytes: half the banks, 4 chunks
rows and cols are the size of the tile to lay out. For Q
width is how many values one row of the pattern holds. If
cols is a multiple of 64, it is 64 values. In bf16 (2
bytes per value) that is 128 bytes: exactly one sweep
Otherwise it is 32 values, 64 bytes: for a tile only 32
wide, such as P when a block takes 32 keys at a time.
The swizzle moves whole chunks: 8 values, 16 bytes, 4
banks. A 64-wide row has 8 chunks, c0 to c7.
Start from a plain block of 8 rows

svg.text: c0 of all 8 rows is in banks 0–3:
reading it takes 8 passes (an 8-way bank conflict).
make_layout((8, width), stride=(width, 1)) is a plain
block of 8 rows, stored one after another (row-major).
Value (r, c) goes to slot 64 r + c.
This is v0's layout. Every row is exactly 128 bytes, so
chunk c0 lands in banks 0–3 in every row, c1 in banks 4–7,
The loads that feed the multiply read the same chunk of 8
rows at once. Here all 8 are in the same banks, so a bank
serves them one at a time: 8 passes (rounds of reading)
Why 8 rows? 8 chunks per row are just enough to give each
of those 8 rows its own banks.
The swizzle: which bits of the slot to mix

svg.text: mix 3 bits: the chunk number, 0 to 7
leave the lowest 3 bits alone: a chunk's 8 values stay together
take the bits to mix in from 3 places higher: row mod 8
Swizzle<3,3,3>. It works on the slot number written in
In a 64-wide row, a slot's bits split in three: the lowest
3 are the value inside its chunk, the next 3 the chunk
number, and the 3 above those the row mod 8 (a row is 64 =
XOR (exclusive or) compares two bits: the same gives 0,
different gives 1. The rule XORs the row bits into the
chunk bits, so each row reorders its chunks in its own
For 32-wide rows the first number is 2: 2 bits, for 4
Join them: the atom, 8 swizzled rows

svg.text: c0 of the 8 rows is now in 8 different groups of banks:
steps: the plain layout turns (row, column) into a slot, 0
is added (an extra shift, unused here), and the swizzle
The result, atom, is the smallest piece of the pattern: 8
Each row keeps its own 8 chunks, only in a new order. Row
0 does not move: XOR with 0 changes nothing.
Repeat the atom to fill the tile

svg.text: tile_to_shape copies the 8 × 64 atom until it covers rows
× cols. The 64 × 64 tile of Q takes 8 copies, stacked
(0, 1) is the fill order, by dimension: dimension 0 (down
the rows) first, then dimension 1 (across the columns). A
64 × 128 tile would fill every row of its left half first,
so its right half starts at slot 4096.
Each atom is 512 values, 1 KB, and repeats the same
pattern. In blue, c0 of each row: one per position, in

svg.text: Same code, same value; only where it sits in shared memory changes.
get_tensor views Q's buffer in shared memory through the
new layout. The comment shows the old one: plain row-
The rest of the kernel does not change: it still asks for
sQ[r, c], row r, column c. Only the slot that request
v1 does the same for K, V and P.
